document_title: The Senate bill names Alaska once.

slides.headline: The Senate bill names Alaska once.
Washington needs the RCA's yes.
slides.body: New Federal Power Act section 224(d) has the Energy Secretary weigh congestion inside Alaska with the State and affected Tribes. It may name an Alaska area only "subject to the approval of the Regulatory Commission of Alaska."
labels: NEW FPA SEC. 224(d)(2) · SENATE TEXT, NOVEMBER 19TH

slides.headline: Everywhere else, comments. In Alaska, a yes.
slides.body: For every other area the Secretary may name congestion after taking comments from affected States and Tribes. No state commission approves. The approval step appears only in the Alaska subsection.

slides.headline: Support thinned. It still passed.
slides.body: On passage, 47 Republicans, 14 Democrats and 1 independent voted yea. Murkowski and Sullivan both voted yea.

slides.headline: "No subsidy of data centers."
slides.body: The section's own heading, further down the same text.

slides.headline: A data center's added cost stays on its own bill.
slides.body: No part of the incremental cost of serving one may be charged to another customer. Recovery continues if it quits early, and the utility collects financial assurance first.

slides.kicker: HOW BIG IS A DATA CENTER?
slides.headline: As introduced, 20 megawatts. As passed, no line at all.
slides.body: S. 5653, introduced September 30th, counted load at 20 megawatts or more. The Senate-passed section 229 defines a data center by what it houses, artificial intelligence included, with no megawatt floor.

slides.kicker: WHAT SECTION 229 LETS A STATE DO
slides.headline: Three tools, if a State picks them up.
slides.body: They apply to sites that connect on or after enactment. "State" includes a State commission, and the section expands no one's jurisdiction.
labels: Bill data centers as their own retail class
Set terms less favorable than for other large loads
Require enough new generation to serve them

slides.headline: It heads to the House.
slides.body: Should the RCA, not Washington, decide where Alaska's grid is congested?

post_copy:
One subsection. That is the only place the Senate's energy bill names Alaska.

Section 224(d) lets the Energy Secretary identify an Alaska congestion area only "subject to the approval of the Regulatory Commission of Alaska." Elsewhere there is no state approval step, only comments.

The Senate passed it 62 to 33 on November 19th. Murkowski and Sullivan voted yea.

Section 229 bars charging other customers any part of a data center's incremental cost. The data center keeps paying if it quits early. A State may bill data centers as their own class on less favorable terms.

The clause in its own words opens the carousel, four Senate roll calls follow, and the data center cost rule closes it.

The bill now heads to the House.
Does the RCA's approval step come back intact?

#AlaskaEnergy #FederalPowerAct #DataCenterPolicy

editor_notes_for_email: Section 224(d) gives the Regulatory Commission of Alaska an approval step over an Alaska congestion finding, not a veto, and the deck and caption word it as approval throughout. Whether section 229 reaches Alaska's intrastate utilities isn't settled by the text (229(e) says it expands and diminishes no one's jurisdiction), so slides 06 to 08 say what the section lets a State do and never that it binds Alaska's utilities. The claim that the RCA regulates Railbelt rates was killed for want of a fetched source, so the RCA's role rests on the bill's own words only, and nothing is claimed about the House beyond NPR's November 20th report that the bill "now heads to the House." The carved clause on 02 is canvas art, and the same words are printed verbatim in that slide's body, so the PDF text layer and screen readers carry it. The routine ran at effort medium, not the high the settings file carries.
